title: Signal and Gravity
premise: Yara Almeida, the last terraformer on half-finished colony world Meridian, tends a greenhouse garden meant for colonists still in cryosleep and maintains a beacon whose original purpose has been lost to bureaucratic decay. When the colony's children begin sharing an identical dream — a voice counting down in a dead language — Yara realizes his beacon isn't broadcasting to Earth at all: it's receiving, and it has been translating an alien signal into their sleep for years. As the colonial authority moves to silence the children and the reactor powering the beacon enters an uncommanded countdown, Yara must choose between the found family he's built among the dreamers and the survival protocols that kept him invisible. In the end, he broadcasts the aliens' true message — an offer of coexistence contingent on humanity abandoning its war fleet inbound to Meridian — ending one war by risking another, and finally claiming a name and a place among the people he was hired to serve.
about_author: Dominic Blackwood is the pen name of a former hydrologist who spent six years on remote research stations before turning to fiction, writing at night under generator hum. Signal and Gravity is his third novel, and the first written after he stopped answering messages from the organization that once employed him.

chapters.title: The Gardener of Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. He tends the greenhouse built for cryo-sleeping colonists, talks to seedlings like they're students, and logs the beacon's routine pulse nobody reads. Establishes his deliberate invisibility and quiet loneliness. Emotional beat: tender melancholy — a man practicing parenthood on plants.

chapters.title: Children Who Dream in Unison
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Nia Okonkwo, age nine, who wakes her parents describing a countdown in a language no one taught her. Three other children report the same dream. The colony doctor dismisses it; Nia's mother doesn't. Emotional beat: creeping unease beneath domestic normalcy.

chapters.title: Maintenance Logs and Ghosts
chapters.summary: Yara discovers anomalous return signals buried in the beacon's noise floor — structured, repeating, old. His records show the anomalies predate his assignment by decades. Someone knew. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing your invisible job was never yours alone.

chapters.title: The Administrator's Quiet War
chapters.summary: Administrator Voss POV. She manages dwindling supplies, a hostile orbital standoff with the rival Halcyon faction, and now reports of shared dreams she files as mass psychogenic illness. Her pragmatism is sympathetic but hardening. Emotional beat: fear wearing the mask of competence.

chapters.title: What the Seedlings Heard
chapters.summary: Yara finds the greenhouse crops growing toward patterns that match the signal's waveform. Nia sneaks into the garden and finishes his sentences about the dream. First real connection in years. Emotional beat: reluctant warmth cracking open isolation.

chapters.title: Decommission Order
chapters.summary: Voss orders the beacon powered down to conserve reactor output for defense systems. Yara stalls, falsifies maintenance schedules, and recruits the station's aging engineer, Bram, who admits he helped build the beacon — and knows what it was really for. Emotional beat: guilt becoming resolve.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession
chapters.summary: Bram reveals the beacon was commissioned to listen, not broadcast: first contact protocol from a program officially erased after the war began. The children aren't sick; they're receivers maturing. Emotional beat: grief for a future betrayed by politics.

chapters.title: Countdown Made Visible
chapters.summary: The reactor begins an uncommanded ramp-down synchronized exactly with the number the children recite. Yara realizes the signal isn't just being received — it's negotiating, using the reactor as leverage. Emotional beat: awe curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Quarantine
chapters.summary: Voss isolates the dreaming children 'for their safety.' Nia's mother begs Yara to intervene. He must decide whether to stay hidden or burn his cover. Emotional beat: the price of neutrality coming due.

chapters.title: Breaking Pattern
chapters.summary: Yara breaks into quarantine, and the act itself — witnessed — shatters his invisibility permanently. He and Nia communicate through the dream's grammar, learning the message is conditional and time-bound. Emotional beat: terror and liberation arriving together.

chapters.title: The Message, Half-Translated
chapters.summary: Working nights with Bram and Nia, Yara decodes fragments: the aliens offer terraforming completion — the very garden he tends — if humanity recalls its war fleet. Refusal means the countdown ends badly. Emotional beat: hope with a knife's edge.

chapters.title: Voss Learns the Truth
chapters.summary: Voss confronts Yara with evidence of his sabotage. Instead of arresting him, she demands proof. He shows her the decoded fragment and her own daughter's dream transcript — Voss's child is among the dreamers. Emotional beat: an adversary discovering she's already inside the story.

chapters.title: Faction Fault Lines
chapters.summary: News leaks. Halcyon accuses Meridian of alien collusion; Meridian hawks call the signal a trap. Voss must choose between reporting up the chain — which triggers fleet escalation — or concealing it, which is treason. Emotional beat: leadership as solitary suffocation.

chapters.title: The Garden as Argument
chapters.summary: Yara leads Voss and skeptical colonists through the greenhouse, showing crops shaped by decades of alien guidance — proof of patient goodwill. The garden meant for the unborn becomes evidence in a trial of intentions. Emotional beat: quiet persuasion outlasting shouting.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: A frightened technician, acting on orders from a hardline faction, damages the beacon array mid-decode. The countdown accelerates. Bram takes radiation exposure repairing it. Emotional beat: sacrifice without guarantee.

chapters.title: Nia's Bargain
chapters.summary: Nia, the strongest receiver, offers to carry a question directly into the dream: can the deadline extend if humanity shows good faith? The answer costs her three days unconscious. Emotional beat: a child bearing adult weight, and the community rallying around her.

chapters.title: Two Fleets, One Sky
chapters.summary: Both human fleets converge on Meridian, each believing the other will strike first. Voss transmits the decoded offer over Yara's objection that it's incomplete — a gamble that could trigger panic. Emotional beat: desperate transparency versus protective secrecy.

chapters.title: Reactor Zero Hour
chapters.summary: With hours left, the final fragment decodes: the aliens require not retreat but a joint landing — humans and their rivals together, unarmed, in the garden. Yara must convince two armed factions to walk into the same field. Emotional beat: the impossible ask made plain.

chapters.title: Walking Into the Field
chapters.summary: Climax. Under the beacon's full voice, soldiers from both fleets — and the children as witnesses — enter the greenhouse as the reactor hits critical threshold. The signal resolves: the countdown was never a threat, but a gestation clock. Emotional beat: held breath breaking into tears.

chapters.title: What Wakes Up
chapters.summary: The terraforming engine activates — the aliens were the planet's previous gardeners, dormant in the crust, and the beacon was their alarm clock. Soil transforms overnight. The war fleets stand down, out of arguments. Emotional beat: wonder displacing fear.

chapters.title: Names We Answer To
chapters.summary: Aftermath. Voss resigns rather than let the cover-up define the new era; Bram recovers; the children teach adults the dream-language. Yara, offered honors, asks instead for a small house beside the greenhouse. Emotional beat: identity chosen, not assigned.

chapters.title: First Planting
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Nia's POV. The cryo-pods open early — the colonists wake to a living world. Nia guides the first newcomers into the garden where Yara waits, no longer invisible, holding seedlings labeled with names. Emotional beat: belonging fulfilled; the garden finally meets its people.
